claim: Gunther 2008 states that the USL Cp equals the synchronous throughput bound of a machine-repairman queue with state-dependent service rate, and that Amdahl's law and Gustafson speedup are corollaries of that bound.
Gunther 2008 calls corollary 1 a lower bound on throughput, namely synchronous throughput, and therefore worst-case scalability.
Gunther 2008 assumes exponential uptime and service (M/M/1//p), one server, mean values and steady state, and says the coherency term needs a state-dependent server.

claim: Gunther 2011 says USL measurements should include at least half a dozen data points for the regression to be statistically meaningful.
Gunther 2011 warns that the predicted USL scalability peak Nc may lie outside any physically attainable system configuration.
Gunther 2011, memcached table 27.2: predicted peak Nc is 6.8121 for version 1.2.8 (alpha 0.0255), 6.6591 for 1.4.1 (alpha 0.0821) and 6.5666 for 1.4.5 (alpha 0.0988).
Gunther 2011: after memcached's cache-lock and statistics changes, the scalability peak moved from Nc = 22 threads to Nc = 48 threads (one server, one case).
Gunther 2011 assumes a closed system with a fixed number of users or threads, throughput measured at several N, and one contended resource with pairwise coherency.

note: Secondary text. Hopp and Spearman (1996) was not opened; treat as textbook grade until read at source.

claim: Choo 2016: WIP above critical WIP adds no throughput but increases cycle time, and WIP below it loses throughput.
note: Secondary text citing Hopp and Spearman (1996); no variability in this statement.

claim: Choo 2016: maximum throughput cannot be achieved by merely setting the target WIP equal to the critical WIP.
note: Secondary text citing Hopp and Spearman (1996).

claim: Choo 2016: cycle time grows steeply with utilisation, with 80 to 85% named as the level where it explodes.
note: Secondary text citing Hopp and Spearman (1996); the 80 to 85% figure is the source's own.
